inline.s: Appendix: A Record of the Auspicious Response of Relics Descending by the Lamp

Since I left home, I have heard that the Buddha's power is inconceivable, the Dharma's power is inconceivable, and the power of sentient beings' minds is inconceivable. These three inconceivable things — now I have seen them with my own eyes. And what was it that I saw? Last spring, not reckoning my own mediocrity and shallowness, in the intervals of reciting the Buddha I composed a treatise named the Buddha-Recitation Samadhi, the Jewel King That Emerges from the World. When the draft was first finished, I entrusted it to the layman Hu Songnian to take to Shanghai for publication. But after he took it away, I again felt shame and regret. I reflected that the treatise-makers of old had all fully awakened and personally realized it; their meaning and reasoning, their words and phrases, were profound and broad, thorough and penetrating; and even then they first requested the blessing of the Three Jewels before setting forth the profound meaning, all of it reaching the marrow and revealing the subtle. Even so, when a treatise was complete they would set it aside for a year or half a year, or two or three years, before having it engraved and circulated. I am an ordinary being laden with karmic hindrances, shallow in knowledge, coarse in literary expression. The draft just completed had many shortcomings; how could I rashly bring it out to the world? Therefore I sent a letter instructing Master Desen to be careful not to publish it, and to wait until it was revised and perfected before printing. Up to recent days, I again carefully revised the original draft, dividing and marking its sections, and it grew all the more easy on the eyes; the cumbersome I deleted, the brief I supplemented. Finally I added a conclusion, entitled 'Protecting the Right and Rescuing the Biased,' for fear that people might doubt: 'the Buddha-name is only six characters; how can it be taken as a school?' Within the text I directly point out that a single phrase of the Buddha-name is the whole of the Buddha-fruit; it can be broad or brief, it can unfold or gather. Broad, it embraces the three repositories; brief, it all returns to the six characters. Unfolded, it pervades the ten directions; gathered, it is drawn back into a single thought. This is precisely what is called 'controlling the six senses, pure thought succeeding in continuity.' Realizing this meaning is like a fisherman spreading his net — what harm that ten thousand threads appear together, and in an instant are gathered by a single cord. The wonder of the Buddha-name is precisely here. Therefore I first offered the treatise before the Buddha, earnestly beseeching the Buddha's blessing and his condescending proof. And making a vow before the Buddha, let me now set out the text of the vow in a few words: 'Your disciple respectfully composed this humble treatise, to offer it widely to fellow practitioners in the ten directions. May I, from this retribution-body of the present life on to the future Buddha-body, thought after thought in continuity, without interruption, always make use of this Buddha-Recitation Samadhi, the Jewel King That Emerges from the World, to benefit widely all fellow practitioners in the ten directions, guiding them all together to return to the Land of Bliss, drawing near the King of Vows, forever enjoying the wondrous bliss.' When this vow was made, after a day or two — it was the night of the third day of the tenth month — I was transcribing the draft under the lamp, and just as I came to the point where the questions and answers of the final conclusion were ending, I felt that some ash had fallen from the lamp onto the paper. I brushed it away with my hand, and felt that it was hard and round. I picked it up with my fingers and pressed firmly, and still it would not break. Bringing it near the lamp and examining it closely, I saw that it was purple and luminous with radiance. Only then did I know — could it not be a relic? Thereupon I placed it in a porcelain cup and offered it before the Buddha. The next day at noon, when the sun was strong, I took it out and examined it with a hand mirror, and saw its brilliance radiant, round like a pearl. It was then shown to the whole temple, clergy and laity alike, each one looking; as reported, its size, color, and light were not all the same. Everyone sighed that it was a rare treasure. Even now it is still kept before the Buddha. But because its body is very small, it is not easy to preserve. Yet I reflected again: my treatise was about to be complete, offered before the Buddha, earnestly beseeching his proof. Now, on the paper following the treatise, I received a relic descending — could this not be the Buddha's way of indicating his proof? Therefore I took up the brush to record it, appending it after the treatise, to inform fellow practitioners, so that all who read this treatise will pay deep attention, and each and every one will arouse right faith.

Recorded by the monk Liaoran, who is fed on gruel and rice at Lingyan, in the Non-retreat Chamber of the Zhen Garden of the Sea of the Buddha's Spring, on the fifteenth day of the tenth month of the thirty-third year of the Republic of China.

Note: from the treatise the Buddha-Recitation Samadhi, the Jewel King That Emerges from the World on to the last of the various texts, in all twenty-three relics were obtained. In size, color, and light each was different; because three were lost, twenty remain at present. Let the clergy and laity who come and go request to view and bow before them, so as to nourish faith and vows, arouse the mind to practice, and together gain the supreme benefit.
Recorded again by Liaoran with pen in hand, on the Buddha's rejoicing day, the day of the monks' self-congratulation (prarana), in the seventh month of the thirty-fifth year of the Republic of China.
Appendix: The Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing Reveals the Buddha-Recitation Samadhi

Someone asked: 'When reciting the Buddha's name one cannot attain single-mindedness; what expedient should one use?' The Bodhisattva said: 'You need only put a stop to thoughts and settle your mind, and recite slowly and steadily. Make the sound accord with the mind, and the mind follow the sound. Reciting for a long time, you will naturally attain the clarity and purity of all thoughts, the mind and its object both extinguished, and enter the Buddha-Recitation Samadhi. In daily practice you must recite much, from a thousand up to ten thousand, with the mind never interrupted; then the faculties are most easily matured. If you forcibly try to make it single, you will never attain it.'

Explanation: 'To put a stop to thoughts and settle the mind' is to let go a single thought, with all conditions utterly silent. Like a bubble merging into water, the true and the false are not two. Then lift up a single call of the Buddha-name and recite slowly and steadily, neither high nor low, neither urgent nor slow. Only make the sound and mind unite; then random thoughts are naturally clarified. Through long practice it becomes one piece, mind and object become one, and without being aware of it one enters the Buddha-Recitation Samadhi. It is like a kernel dwelling within the fruit, real and full, unmoving as thusness. Thought following thought without interruption, the faculties are most easily matured. If you forcibly try to make it single, you will never attain it. This passage is a simple, direct, profound, and ultimate instruction, which the wise and the foolish alike can practice. May all readers pay deep heartfelt attention and, in accordance with the Dharma, cultivate by perfume-drenching — the benefit is immeasurable.
Entering the Chamber of Fragrance and Light, Lower Collection
Record of Instructions from the Lingyan Single-Mind Buddha-Recitation Retreat
One Who Wishes to Enter the Fruit-Sea of Samadhi Should First Know Grace and Recompense Grace

All we who practice the Buddha-recitation, wishing to enter the fruit-sea of Amitabha Buddha's samadhi, should first know grace and recompense grace. If one can know grace and recompense grace, then while rightly reciting the Buddha one will at once feel close to Amitabha Buddha's samadhi fruit-sea. Whenever one recollects, it is immediately present. With a single thought present, one realizes that one's own body is originally within Amitabha Buddha's samadhi sea, neither going out nor coming in, dwelling at ease in right samadhi. Naturally thought after thought accords with the Buddha's fruit-sea, mind after mind unites with it. When the accord reaches the utmost, it finally becomes one piece. When a single thought becomes one piece, unmoving as thusness, real and full, it fills the Dharma-realm. Why? Because being able to know grace and recompense grace, one feels that within the Buddha's samadhi sea one must see the Buddha in every thought [see the Dharmakaya of the Buddha], and draw near to the Buddha in every mind [draw near to the Dharmakaya of the Buddha]; if one wished to leave it, it would be utterly impossible. It is like a filial child in the world, who his whole life dares not stay far from his parents; even after his parents have died, he still remembers them thought after thought — all because of knowing grace and recompensing grace. Practitioners of the Buddha-recitation should likewise be so. If one does not know grace and recompense grace, though one recites the Buddha all day, one cannot but turn away from the Buddha and be separated from the Buddha. Why? Because being unable to know grace and recompense grace, one feels that Amitabha Buddha dwells in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, separated by a hundred thousand koti of lands, as if wholly unrelated to oneself. Though the mouth recites the Buddha, the mind is in fact reluctant; hence, while rightly reciting the Buddha, one's thoughts inevitably flow onward, and the mind inevitably wanders in distraction. One cannot dwell in the Buddha's samadhi right samadhi, nor accord with the Buddha's fruit-sea real mark. It is like an unfilial child, thought after thought keeping far from his parents, mind after mind going against his home village.

What is meant by knowing grace and recompensing grace? You should know that Amitabha Buddha, through countless kalpas, has been our heavenly compassionate father. We, through countless kalpas, have also been Amitabha Buddha's kinsfolk of one substance. Through the kalpas our life of wisdom has been joined, father and son mutually bound; it is not a chance reliance or a forced taking of refuge. Amitabha Buddha's grace and virtue toward us sentient beings surpass that of our own birth-parents by a hundred thousand million times. Even to the end of the future, with counting and with simile, one cannot exhaust it. Why? Because although our parents' grace and virtue toward us is great, in the end they can think of us for only one lifetime. But Amitabha Buddha is mindful of us sentient beings through endless kalpas without exhaustion. It is said: though sentient beings do not recite the Buddha, the Buddha is always mindful of sentient beings. Moreover, although parents are compassionate and educate us, pitying and protecting us, they can only hope that I become an accomplished person in the world. But Shakyamuni Tathagata's compassionate education and Amitabha Buddha's pitying protection directly hope that I will end birth and death, transcend the ordinary and enter the holy, even to Buddhahood, and only then rest. Moreover, parents can only gather me in their physical body and protect me by the power of the mind. The Buddha can gather me in his Dharmakaya and protect me by the power of his spiritual powers. And parents can only give birth to my physical body; the Buddha can give birth to my Dharmakaya.

What is meant by 'heavenly compassionate father' and 'kinsfolk of one substance'? Amitabha Buddha, in the past countless kalpas ago, when he aroused the great bodhi-mind, originally aroused it for us. When he abandoned the throne of the wheel-turning king, he abandoned it for us. When he went forth from home under the Buddha Lokêsvara-raja, he left home for us. At his first going forth he was named Dharmakara Bhikshu; pitying us and all beings in the ten directions, with compassionate eyes he regarded them equally, as if loving a single child. Originally he was of the same true awakened mind as us, without duality or difference. But because we have been deluded, we are unaware and unknowing. Therefore Dharmakara Bhikshu, within his true awakened real mind, at once arose in the unconditioned great compassion and set to work the great compassion of one substance, and before the Buddha Lokêsvara-raja established the forty-eight great vows — originally establishing them for us. Then, through kalpas as many as dust, he cultivated immeasurable pure and wondrous practices — originally cultivating them for us. He adorned the four kinds of Pure Land — originally adorning them for us. Until merit and wisdom were fulfilled and every vow perfectly accomplished, and only then did he realize right enlightenment in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss — originally realizing it for us. The great name of ten thousand virtues is called Amitabha. You should know that the Tathagata's great name was accomplished by the power of his vows in former lives. He extended this expedient to guide sentient beings, causing them to take the name as their point of entry, saving all beings universally and returning them together to the Land of Bliss. From this they advance in practice and together verify the Buddha-fruit. This grace, this virtue — heaven, earth, and parents could not express a ten-thousandth of it.

Now let me trace back its origin. In the past, Dharmakara Bhikshu, before he had aroused the resolve, was originally, like us, an ordinary being. Because after arousing the resolve he left home life life after life and cultivated age after age, he therefore attained Buddhahood early. The Amitabha Sutra says: It has now been ten kalpas since Amitabha Buddha attained Buddhahood. The Buddha is never for a single moment not mindful of us. But alas, from beginningless time we have always been deluded. Because of this, life after life we create karma, age after age we fall. Sometimes we are in hell, undergoing all kinds of intense suffering; sometimes in the realm of hungry ghosts, burning with the fire of hunger; sometimes among animals, supplying the mouths and bellies of people. Often, for many tens of thousands of kalpas, we do not hear the names of the Buddhas. Even if we leave the three evil paths, we may be among the asuras, angry, hateful, and fighting; or in the heaven realm, clinging to pleasures. Even if among humans, we may be born before or after a Buddha, or in border lands of lowly birth — solitary and poor, hungry and cold, distressed and afflicted, stupid and dull, deaf, dumb, blind, and mute, with the six faculties incomplete, sickly and short-lived. Even if we have abundant food and clothing and complete faculties, we may not believe in the Three Jewels and create much evil karma. Though we believe in the Three Jewels, we may not recognize right from wrong and additionally practice non-Buddhist paths. Though we do not believe what is wrong, we may be solely greedy for blessings. Even if we cultivate both merit and wisdom, we may not believe in the Pure Land. Though we believe in the Pure Land, we may half-believe and half-doubt. Or we believe but do not vow; or vow but do not practice; or practice but not single-mindedly. Though willing to practice single-mindedly, we may not encounter a good friend and so lack progress. All these various hindrances are because our conditions are incomplete; the pure karma is hard to accomplish, and birth and death are not ended. Therefore, through countless kalpas, we are always in the Saha world, transmigrating in the six paths, undergoing all kinds of suffering without rest. The Buddha in his compassion is mindful of us, but we are unaware and unknowing. Now that we have come to hear and know this, we should arouse great shame and remorse, weeping tears like rain, thirsting for our compassionate father, seeking to see him thought after thought, never forgetting him mind after mind. How do we seek to see him? How do we not forget? Now we have fortunately obtained a human body and are born in the central land; though we do not encounter the Buddha in person, we rely on meeting the clear texts of the teaching. We further are able to draw near a good friend, who reveals the Pure Land Dharma-gate — direct and steady, simple and easy to practice, not requiring many lifetimes, able to be settled in the present life.

As for 'meeting the clear texts of the teaching' — that is the Amitabha Sutra spoken by the Buddha. This sutra is concise in wording yet complete in principle and fact. The World-Honored One Shakyamuni, with a thoroughly compassionate heart, pitying us heavily-obstructed ordinary beings of the last age, who cannot by our own power awaken the mind and reach the origin, break off delusion and verify the truth, specially extended an expedient and, unasked, spoke it himself, disclosing it fully without concealing the slightest. First he spoke of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the splendor of its dependent and proper retribution. Next he taught the arising of faith and the making of vows. Having faith and vows, one should arouse true practice — holding the great name of ten thousand virtues, hoping to attain single-mindedness. This single-mindedness is the original awakening that is the common source of sages and ordinary beings, the true mind co-substantial with beings and Buddhas. When Amitabha Buddha first aroused the bodhi-mind, it was this mind he aroused. When he established the forty-eight vows, each and every one was established in dependence on this mind. Then, in kalpas as many as dust, when he cultivated immeasurable wondrous practices, each and every one was cultivated in dependence on this mind. When he adorned the four kinds of Pure Land, each and every one was adorned in dependence on this mind. Until merit and wisdom were fulfilled and he perfectly verified the supreme samadhi fruit-sea — that too was the perfect verification of this mind. We, through countless kalpas, submerged and drifting, losing our way and falling, life after life — what we lost was this mind. Up to the present life, though we have gained a human body and a slight acquaintance with the Dharma, we still cannot awaken the mind and reach the origin, break off delusion and verify the truth, end birth and death, transcend the ordinary and enter the holy. Therefore we entirely rely on the great name of ten thousand virtues accomplished by Amitabha Buddha's vow-power in former lives, borrowed as our point of entry, drawn into the Tathagata's fruit-sea real mark, dwelling at ease in the Tathagata's samadhi right samadhi. We need only harbor utmost sincerity thought after thought, and call upon the Buddha's name. This can cause thought after thought to turn away from the dust and unite with awareness, to return from the false to the true — like a river entering the sea, gradually entering, gradually deepening. It is said: a single thought of utmost sincerity, then a single thought enters the Buddha's real mark; thought after thought of utmost sincerity, then thought after thought enters the Buddha's real mark. And a single thought not flowing, not wandering — then a single thought dwells in the Buddha's right samadhi; thought after thought not flowing, not wandering — then thought after thought dwells in the Buddha's right samadhi. If one can use the mind thus thought after thought, and reflect and illuminate thus, treading solid ground step by step, then from here on, reciting the Buddha, every phrase is powerful, every character flows from the Tathagata's real-mark right samadhi. It is said: the real mark is the great name, the great name is the real mark. Long-cultivated and matured, it needs no forcing. Though there are deluded thoughts flowing, in one moment of awareness they return. Though there are habitual tendencies wandering, in one illumination they cease. According with the original source, unmoving as thusness, real and full, it fills the Dharma-realm. Having entered the Tathagata's samadhi fruit-sea, one constantly receives the Tathagata's Dharmakaya nurture, his compassionate mind's protection, his samadhi power's upholding, the real mark's fusion, the wisdom-light's shining through, and the power of wisdom's penetrating clarity. This causes our countless-kalpas defilements of the six objects and the hindrances of the five aggregates gradually to dissolve, all transforming into the Tathagata's fruit-sea great-light treasury, wholly transparent, becoming a single color. Even if in the present life we cannot cut off entirely the outflows of views and thought, or in part break through subtle ignorance and personally verify the Tathagata's fruit-sea real mark, we can still by this reduce our flowing, dwell in the Buddha's right samadhi, and personally draw near the real mark. Like one who perfumes himself with incense — his body bears the fragrance. With this merit, we direct it to the West and make the vow to be reborn. Until the Saha retribution is exhausted and the Western conditions are ripe, the sublime realm of Ultimate Bliss will naturally manifest within the Buddha's fruit-sea light treasury. Then surely the compassionate father Amitabha and the holy assembly will personally descend to guide us, and we will be reborn in the Land of Bliss. As it is said: father and son through the kalpas, seeing each other in a single morning — what consolation! Relying on the Buddha's spiritual power, in a mere snap of the fingers we arrive. Having arrived in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, we return together to the seven-jewel lotus pool. When the flower opens and we see the Buddha, hearing the Buddha's teaching we are awakened, drawing near to the unsurpassed compassionate father and the pure sea of the assembly. We study and practice all Dharma-gates, accomplishing the power of patient endurance in non-arising, endowed with the five eyes and the six supernatural powers, perfecting the three bodies and the four wisdoms. Without moving the subtle wonderful body, we manifest immeasurable countless transformation bodies, always carrying out the Tathagata's commission, guiding in the ten directions the deluded multitudes, bringing them all back to the Lotus Land, together verifying the fruit-sea bodhi. The above is what is meant by 'one who wishes to enter the Tathagata's samadhi fruit-sea should first know grace and recompense grace' — a brief account of it is thus.
